Verisimilar

vair-ih-SIM-ih-lar · adjective

What It Means

Verisimilar is having the appearance of being true or real.

Museum curators worked hard to make the wax figures verisimilar down to the smallest wrinkle.

Worked Example

The video game's city felt so verisimilar that players kept forgetting it wasn't a real place.

A fictional city so convincing that players forget it's fake is exactly verisimilar.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

plausible: Plausible judges likelihood: a plausible excuse or theory is one that could reasonably be true. Verisimilar judges texture instead — how closely something wears the look and detail of real life — and a story can be verisimilar while its events stay impossible.

lifelike: Lifelike praises a visual copy for resembling the living original — a wax figure, a portrait, an animation. Verisimilar reaches wider: prose, a stage performance, a game world can all be verisimilar, true-seeming in their detail without copying any one real thing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

far-fetched: so unlikely it is hard to believe

Where it sits · how closely it mirrors actual life — believable → verisimilar → photorealistic

believable vs. verisimilar: Believable simply means a person could accept it as true, a mild everyday word; verisimilar specifically praises how closely something resembles reality in its details.

photorealistic vs. verisimilar: Photorealistic pushes lifelike detail to an almost literal, photograph-level extreme, while verisimilar can apply to writing or performance, not just images.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — veri

root — veri: true (Latin (verus))

root — simil

root — simil: like, similar (Latin (similis))

suffix — -ar

suffix — -ar: having the quality of (Latin (-aris))

Put it together

Put it together: Verisimilar combines Latin verus ('true') + similis ('like') -- literally 'like the truth.'

Use the root in a new word: verify

Use the root in a new word: verify: The same verus root gives us the everyday word verify, to confirm something is true -- both words are built on that same idea of truth.
